screens.title: Introduction to DApps and Their Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we will explore what a Decentralized Application, or DApp, really is and why it changes the rules for host, control, and trust. A DApp moves backend logic and data off a single company server and onto a peer-to-peer network, typically a blockchain. That shift gives DApps four defining advantages you should remember: decentralization, open-source transparency, immutability of deployed logic, and resistance to censorship. You will see concrete examples of each idea and how common components — a familiar web frontend, a web3 library, on-chain smart contracts, the blockchain ledger, and decentralized storage networks — combine into a working architecture. We will contrast this with how a traditional client-server web app behaves so you can spot trade-offs quickly. By the end you will be able to identify the essential parts of a DApp, name a practical use case such as a decentralized exchange or NFT marketplace, and explain when off-chain storage is appropriate. Think about a problem you know: could removing a central operator make it fairer, more resilient, or more transparent?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will develop four practical competencies that map to designing, evaluating, and using DApps. First, you will be able to articulate the core characteristics and benefits of DApps — decentralization, transparency, immutability, and censorship resistance — and explain why those qualities matter for trust and resilience. Second, you will be able to compare DApps to traditional centralized applications, identifying where control, failure modes, and data custody differ and what trade-offs arise. Third, you will identify the essential technical components that make up a DApp: the frontend, web3 library, smart contracts as on-chain logic, the blockchain ledger, and decentralized storage options. Fourth, you will recognize common real-world applications and use cases — for example, DeFi protocols like lending and swaps, NFT marketplaces, and DAOs — and explain briefly how decentralization shapes each use case. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember and a verified competency milestone to test your understanding.

screens.title: What is a Decentralized Application (DApp)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Decentralized Application, or DApp, is an application whose backend logic and often its data run on a decentralized peer-to-peer network, usually a blockchain. Put simply, instead of a single company server controlling code and data, the DApp’s rules are encoded in smart contracts on a ledger replicated across many nodes. A concrete example is a decentralized exchange: the swap logic lives in smart contracts, and trades execute according to those on-chain rules without a central matching server. A common misconception is that a DApp must be entirely on-chain; in practice, many DApps pair a regular web frontend with on-chain contracts and decentralized or off-chain storage for large files. That hybrid model preserves user experience while keeping core rules and state public and tamper-resistant. Why this matters: business logic enforced on-chain creates predictable behavior and removes single-operator censorship or unilateral changes. A quick contrast helps cement the idea — in a centralized social media app the company can change moderation rules overnight; in a DApp the moderation or governance may be enforced by smart contracts and community voting, so changes follow the on-chain process. To check your understanding, ask: what part of an app would you not want to be immutable on-chain, and why?

keyIdea.title: DApp defined
keyIdea.text: A DApp runs backend logic on a peer-to-peer network via smart contracts, replacing single-operator control with verifiable, distributed execution.

content.html:
Definition What is a DApp?

Working definition

An application that runs backend logic on a decentralized peer-to-peer network, using smart contracts and often decentralized storage, rather than relying on a single centralized server.

Concrete example
A decentralized exchange executes swaps via smart contracts on-chain; no central matching engine controls trades.
Common misconception
Not every part of a DApp must be on-chain; UIs and large media files are typically off-chain for performance and cost reasons.
Key Takeaway

DApps shift trust from an operator to verifiable code and a distributed ledger, while still using familiar frontends for user interaction.

Contrast: Centralized App vs DApp
Centralized App
  • Backend hosted on company servers
  • Company controls policy and data
  • Single point of failure
DApp
  • Backend logic in smart contracts
  • State replicated on many nodes
  • Harder to censor or alter rules
Check your understanding: which part of an application benefits most from on-chain immutability, and which parts are better kept off-chain?

screens.title: The Four Defining Characteristics of DApps
screens.narratorSegment: DApps are often described by four defining characteristics that explain their value. First, decentralization: there is no single point of control because logic and state live across many nodes. This reduces single-point failures and concentrates trust in code and consensus rather than an operator. Second, open-source code: many DApps publish their code so users, auditors, and community members can inspect and contribute, which builds confidence and enables community-driven development. Third, immutability: smart contracts deployed on-chain cannot be altered by one actor; their rules remain consistent unless the contract itself includes an on-chain upgrade mechanism. This predictability is essential for financial protocols and governance. Fourth, censorship resistance: DApps running on public blockchains are difficult for any single authority to shut down, increasing availability for users. A concrete example: a lending protocol that publishes its smart contracts, runs interest and collateral rules on-chain, and stores metadata in decentralized storage — users can verify behavior and continue using core services even if original developers disengage. A common misconception is that these characteristics remove all risk; they reduce centralized control but introduce new considerations like immutable bugs and economic attack vectors. Reflect: which characteristic matters most for the problem you care about?

keyIdea.title: Four pillars
keyIdea.text: These four properties—decentralization, open-source code, immutability, and censorship resistance—explain why DApps change trust models and resilience.

content.html:
Core Concept

The four defining characteristics

Understand each property and how it affects design choices and risks.

Decentralization
Backend logic and state are replicated across nodes, preventing single-operator control and increasing resilience to outages.
Open-source
Public code allows inspection, auditing, and community contributions, increasing trust and transparency.
Immutability
Deployed smart contracts enforce rules that cannot be changed by a single party, ensuring consistent behavior over time.
Censorship resistance
Running on public, distributed networks makes it difficult for authorities or operators to shut down access to the application.
Key Takeaway

These properties shift trust from centralized operators to code and consensus, but they also create new technical and governance trade-offs.

Concrete scenario

Imagine a lending DApp: interest calculation and liquidation rules run in smart contracts, collateral records live on-chain, and the UI uses a web3 library to submit transactions. With open-source code, auditors can verify safety. With immutability, users can trust rules but must also handle discovered bugs carefully.

Common error: assuming immutability means the system is bug-free. In fact, immutable bugs require governance or upgrade patterns to address safely.

screens.title: Anatomy of a DApp
screens.narratorSegment: A DApp's architecture is a layered system combining familiar frontend technologies with blockchain-specific components. Start with the frontend: a normal web interface built with H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript provides the user experience. Instead of calling a centralized A P I, the frontend uses a web3 library to form transactions and read on-chain state. The web3 library is a bridge: it encodes calls to smart contracts, submits signed transactions, and reads ledger data. Smart contracts are the on-chain backend — self-executing programs that define rules, state transitions, and events. The blockchain itself stores contract code and state, providing immutability and consensus for execution. For large files or off-chain metadata, DApps use decentralized storage networks like IPFS or Arweave to avoid storing bulky data on-chain. A concrete example: an NFT marketplace uses a web UI to display art, a smart contract to transfer ownership and record token metadata, and IPFS to host the artwork file. A common misconception is that the blockchain stores all data; storing large media on-chain is expensive and unnecessary. The practical question for design becomes: which state must be on-chain to preserve guarantees, and which can be stored in a decentralized but off-chain service to save cost and maintain availability?

keyIdea.title: Layered architecture
keyIdea.text: DApps mix a standard frontend and web3 library with smart contracts on a blockchain ledger and decentralized storage for large or off-chain data.

content.html:
Architecture

DApp architecture layers

Layered components
Frontend
Standard web UI that builds the user experience and collects signatures for transactions.
Web3 library
A client-side library that creates and signs transactions and reads on-chain state.
Smart contracts
On-chain programs that define application rules and manipulate state deterministically.
Blockchain ledger
A replicated database and execution environment that provides immutability and consensus.
Decentralized storage
IPFS or Arweave for large files and off-chain metadata to keep data decentralized without on-chain cost.
Annotated example
NFT marketplace:
  • Frontend shows items and signs purchase transactions.
  • Web3 library encodes transaction for the marketplace contract.
  • Smart contract transfers token ownership and emits events.
  • Artwork files live on IPFS and metadata references the IPFS hash.
Key Takeaway

Design decisions hinge on which state and rules require on-chain guarantees versus which can remain off-chain to save cost and improve UX.

screens.title: When to Put Logic On-Chain vs Off-Chain
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding what belongs on-chain is a central design decision for DApps. On-chain logic gives strong guarantees: transparency, immutability, and verifiable execution. That makes it ideal for things like token transfers, settlement rules, and governance where trust in correct execution is essential. However, on-chain operations have costs and performance limits. Storing large files or doing compute-heavy processing on-chain is expensive and slow. Off-chain or decentralized off-chain approaches are useful for heavy computation, indexing, user-friendly search, and hosting large media. For example, an NFT marketplace keeps the artwork itself on IPFS and only stores the token metadata hash on-chain. A common misconception is that moving logic off-chain removes trust completely; instead, designers often use a hybrid model where critical state and final settlement remain on-chain while helper services run off-chain with clear interfaces. Upgradeability is another factor: immutable contracts cannot be changed, so many teams plan upgrade patterns and governance processes before deployment. When you design a DApp ask: do users require on-chain proof for this action? If yes, implement it on-chain. If not, prefer off-chain approaches to reduce cost and complexity.

keyIdea.title: On-chain vs Off-chain
keyIdea.text: Place only the rules and state that demand verifiable, tamper-proof guarantees on-chain; keep heavy data and computation off-chain or in decentralized storage.

content.html:
Comparison

On-chain vs Off-chain decisions

When to choose on-chain
  • Actions requiring verifiable settlement (token transfers, trades)
  • Governance votes where immutability matters
  • Critical state whose tamper-proof history must be public
Example: token swap settlement and liquidity accounting belong on-chain to prevent fraud and ensure correctness.
When to choose off-chain
  • Large media files and bulky datasets
  • Compute-heavy processing and real-time indexing
  • UX features that need low latency
Example: store artwork on IPFS and record only its content hash on-chain to link file and token ownership.
Pro tip

Plan upgrade and governance strategies before deployment to handle immutable bugs and evolving requirements.

screens.title: Smart Contracts: The On-Chain Backend
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contracts are self-executing programs stored and run on a blockchain that define state transitions, events, and business rules for a DApp. They act as the authoritative backend: when certain conditions are met, the smart contract updates state or emits events. A concrete example is a liquidity pool contract that updates token balances when swaps are executed and enforces fee rules automatically. A frequent misconception is that smart contracts are like legal contracts; they are code-first and must be thoroughly audited because once deployed their behavior is immutable unless explicit upgrade paths are built in. This immutability creates trust in predictable execution but also means bugs can be permanent or costly. Designing smart contracts requires careful consideration of edge cases, clear failure modes, and well-defined access controls. The practical skill is to decide which operations require on-chain enforcement and to design contracts with events and interfaces that make off-chain integration straightforward. To deepen your understanding, inspect a simple contract: observe how functions change state and emit events that a frontend or indexer can consume. Smart Contracts: The On-Chain Backend means smart contracts encode the immutable application logic and state transitions that form the dapp's authoritative backend on-chain.. In practical terms, what smart contracts are and how they enforce application rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Smart contract role
keyIdea.text: Smart contracts encode the immutable application logic and state transitions that form the DApp's authoritative backend on-chain.

content.html:
Definition

Smart Contracts explained

Smart contracts are programs deployed to the blockchain that automatically execute defined behavior when called. They maintain state variables, run functions, and emit events that off-chain services can watch.
Concrete example
A liquidity pool contract updates balances and enforces swap math and fee distribution without a central operator.
Misconception
Immutable contracts are not bug-proof. If a contract has a flaw, remediation requires pre-planned upgrade patterns or governance actions.
Inspection prompt

When reading a contract, look for public functions that change state, events that emit important changes, and any owner or admin controls that could affect immutability.

Key Takeaway

Smart contracts provide on-chain guarantees but require careful design, audits, and upgrade strategies to manage immutable behavior safely.

screens.title: Decentralized Storage: When and How to Use It
screens.narratorSegment: Decentralized storage solutions like IPFS and Arweave let DApps keep large files and media off-chain while preserving decentralization and censorship resistance. Blockchains are poor places for bulky data because of cost and replication constraints; instead, DApps store content in peer-to-peer storage and record a content hash or pointer on-chain. For example, an NFT contract can store token metadata or art on IPFS and include the content identifier in the token's metadata field. This approach keeps ownership and provenance verifiable on-chain while avoiding high storage costs. A common mistake is trusting a single gateway or node to host content; decentralized storage requires content to be pinned or otherwise made widely available to ensure long-term persistence. Another practical point: content addressing via hashes provides integrity — if the content changes, the hash changes, so the on-chain pointer remains valid only for the original file. When designing storage for a DApp, decide which assets must be persistent and who or what will guarantee availability, such as pinning services or distributed incentives. Decentralized Storage: When and How to Use It means use decentralized storage to host large files and keep the blockchain for authoritative references, ensuring integrity through content addressing while managing availability separately.. In practical terms, ipfs, arweave, and linking off-chain data to on-chain state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use decentralized storage to host large files and keep the blockchain for authoritative references, ensuring integrity through content addressing while managing availability separately.

content.html:
Definition

Decentralized storage in DApps

Use IPFS or Arweave to host large files and store only a content identifier or hash on-chain. This preserves integrity and links off-chain data to the ledger.
Concrete example
An NFT stores its artwork on IPFS and saves the IPFS hash in the token metadata; ownership changes occur on-chain, while the file is retrieved from IPFS.
Common mistake
Relying on a single gateway or node risks content loss; ensure pinning or distributed availability strategies.
Design checklist
  • Which assets need immutable provenance?
  • Who will guarantee availability (pinning, nodes, incentives)?
  • How will you reference content hashes from smart contracts?
Key Takeaway

Keep large and mutable data off-chain while anchoring integrity on-chain via content hashes and plan availability strategies up front.

screens.title: How a DApp Transaction Flows End-to-End
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the lifecycle of a typical DApp transaction helps you design correct interactions and anticipate latency and cost. When a user initiates an action in the frontend, the UI collects necessary inputs and asks the user's wallet to sign a transaction. The web3 library formats the call to the appropriate smart contract function and the signed transaction is submitted to the blockchain network. Once the network reaches consensus and includes the transaction in a block, the smart contract executes and updates on-chain state; events are emitted to mark the change. Off-chain indexers or the frontend watch these events to update UI state. keyIdea.title: Transaction lifecycle
keyIdea.text: A DApp transaction moves from UI input to wallet-signed transaction, on-chain execution, event emission, and off-chain indexer or UI update; large files are handled by decentralized storage and referenced on-chain.

content.html:
Process Flow

DApp transaction lifecycle

  1. User action: User clicks purchase or submit and enters required inputs.
  2. Wallet sign: The frontend asks the wallet to sign the transaction payload.
  3. Submit: Web3 library submits signed transaction to the network.
  4. Consensus and execution: Nodes include the transaction in a block and run the smart contract logic.
  5. Event emission: Contract emits events that off-chain services and the frontend consume.
  6. Off-chain update: Indexers or the UI update their state; if needed, IPFS content is fetched using the on-chain hash.
Concrete example

Buying an NFT: sign purchase transaction, wait for confirmations, contract transfers token, event notifies marketplace UI, frontend fetches artwork from IPFS using on-chain hash.

Misconception: treating a pending transaction as final. Design UI to show pending, confirmed, and final states clearly.
Pro tip

Display transaction progress and expected confirmation time so users understand latency and avoid duplicate actions.

Use Cases

Where DApps are used today

DeFi
Lending, borrowing, swaps, and insurance run via smart contracts so users interact without intermediaries.
Example: decentralized exchanges and lending protocols.
NFTs
Marketplaces and token standards prove ownership and provenance for unique digital items.
Example: marketplaces that store art off-chain and ownership on-chain.
DAOs
Organizations governed by token-based voting and smart contract enforced decisions.
Example: community governance for protocol upgrades.
Gaming
On-chain item ownership and provable scarcity for play-to-own experiences.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson we will explore what a Decentralized Application, or DApp, really is and why it changes the rules for host, control, and trust. A DApp moves backend logic and data off a single company server and onto a peer-to-peer network, typically a blockchain. That shift gives DApps four defining advantages you should remember: decentralization, open-source transparency, immutability of deployed logic, and resistance to censorship. You will see concrete examples of each idea and how common components — a familiar web frontend, a web3 library, on-chain smart contracts, the blockchain ledger, and decentralized storage networks — combine into a working architecture. We will contrast this with how a traditional client-server web app behaves so you can spot trade-offs quickly. By the end you will be able to identify the essential parts of a DApp, name a practical use case such as a decentralized exchange or NFT marketplace, and explain when off-chain storage is appropriate. Think about a problem you know: could removing a central operator make it fairer, more resilient, or more transparent?

In this chapter you will develop four practical competencies that map to designing, evaluating, and using DApps. First, you will be able to articulate the core characteristics and benefits of DApps — decentralization, transparency, immutability, and censorship resistance — and explain why those qualities matter for trust and resilience. Second, you will be able to compare DApps to traditional centralized applications, identifying where control, failure modes, and data custody differ and what trade-offs arise. Third, you will identify the essential technical components that make up a DApp: the frontend, web3 library, smart contracts as on-chain logic, the blockchain ledger, and decentralized storage options. Fourth, you will recognize common real-world applications and use cases — for example, DeFi protocols like lending and swaps, NFT marketplaces, and DAOs — and explain briefly how decentralization shapes each use case. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember and a verified competency milestone to test your understanding.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and assessment. You will research and compare two existing DApps in a category you choose, answering questions about the problem they solve, which blockchains they operate on, their core features, and how they leverage decentralization. This activity trains you to inspect smart contract addresses, recognize on-chain features, and evaluate decentralization levels. In assessment, you will answer conceptual questions, such as identifying which characteristic is not a defining DApp property, and explain why web3 libraries are required for frontend-blockchain interactions. Practically, this builds the habit of mapping architecture to user value: why a lending protocol might place interest logic on-chain, or why large media files are better stored off-chain. A short reflection comparing two DApps will help you synthesize trade-offs in user experience, features, and governance. These exercises reinforce the chapter objectives and prepare you to design or critique DApp architectures.

A Decentralized Application, or DApp, is an application whose backend logic and often its data run on a decentralized peer-to-peer network, usually a blockchain. Put simply, instead of a single company server controlling code and data, the DApp’s rules are encoded in smart contracts on a ledger replicated across many nodes. A concrete example is a decentralized exchange: the swap logic lives in smart contracts, and trades execute according to those on-chain rules without a central matching server. A common misconception is that a DApp must be entirely on-chain; in practice, many DApps pair a regular web frontend with on-chain contracts and decentralized or off-chain storage for large files. That hybrid model preserves user experience while keeping core rules and state public and tamper-resistant. Why this matters: business logic enforced on-chain creates predictable behavior and removes single-operator censorship or unilateral changes. A quick contrast helps cement the idea — in a centralized social media app the company can change moderation rules overnight; in a DApp the moderation or governance may be enforced by smart contracts and community voting, so changes follow the on-chain process. To check your understanding, ask: what part of an app would you not want to be immutable on-chain, and why?

DApps are often described by four defining characteristics that explain their value. First, decentralization: there is no single point of control because logic and state live across many nodes. This reduces single-point failures and concentrates trust in code and consensus rather than an operator. Second, open-source code: many DApps publish their code so users, auditors, and community members can inspect and contribute, which builds confidence and enables community-driven development. Third, immutability: smart contracts deployed on-chain cannot be altered by one actor; their rules remain consistent unless the contract itself includes an on-chain upgrade mechanism. This predictability is essential for financial protocols and governance. Fourth, censorship resistance: DApps running on public blockchains are difficult for any single authority to shut down, increasing availability for users. A concrete example: a lending protocol that publishes its smart contracts, runs interest and collateral rules on-chain, and stores metadata in decentralized storage — users can verify behavior and continue using core services even if original developers disengage. A common misconception is that these characteristics remove all risk; they reduce centralized control but introduce new considerations like immutable bugs and economic attack vectors. Reflect: which characteristic matters most for the problem you care about?

A DApp's architecture is a layered system combining familiar frontend technologies with blockchain-specific components. Start with the frontend: a normal web interface built with H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript provides the user experience. Instead of calling a centralized A P I, the frontend uses a web3 library to form transactions and read on-chain state. The web3 library is a bridge: it encodes calls to smart contracts, submits signed transactions, and reads ledger data. Smart contracts are the on-chain backend — self-executing programs that define rules, state transitions, and events. The blockchain itself stores contract code and state, providing immutability and consensus for execution. For large files or off-chain metadata, DApps use decentralized storage networks like IPFS or Arweave to avoid storing bulky data on-chain. A concrete example: an NFT marketplace uses a web UI to display art, a smart contract to transfer ownership and record token metadata, and IPFS to host the artwork file. A common misconception is that the blockchain stores all data; storing large media on-chain is expensive and unnecessary. The practical question for design becomes: which state must be on-chain to preserve guarantees, and which can be stored in a decentralized but off-chain service to save cost and maintain availability?

Deciding what belongs on-chain is a central design decision for DApps. On-chain logic gives strong guarantees: transparency, immutability, and verifiable execution. That makes it ideal for things like token transfers, settlement rules, and governance where trust in correct execution is essential. However, on-chain operations have costs and performance limits. Storing large files or doing compute-heavy processing on-chain is expensive and slow. Off-chain or decentralized off-chain approaches are useful for heavy computation, indexing, user-friendly search, and hosting large media. For example, an NFT marketplace keeps the artwork itself on IPFS and only stores the token metadata hash on-chain. A common misconception is that moving logic off-chain removes trust completely; instead, designers often use a hybrid model where critical state and final settlement remain on-chain while helper services run off-chain with clear interfaces. Upgradeability is another factor: immutable contracts cannot be changed, so many teams plan upgrade patterns and governance processes before deployment. When you design a DApp ask: do users require on-chain proof for this action? If yes, implement it on-chain. If not, prefer off-chain approaches to reduce cost and complexity.

Smart contracts are self-executing programs stored and run on a blockchain that define state transitions, events, and business rules for a DApp. They act as the authoritative backend: when certain conditions are met, the smart contract updates state or emits events. A concrete example is a liquidity pool contract that updates token balances when swaps are executed and enforces fee rules automatically. A frequent misconception is that smart contracts are like legal contracts; they are code-first and must be thoroughly audited because once deployed their behavior is immutable unless explicit upgrade paths are built in. This immutability creates trust in predictable execution but also means bugs can be permanent or costly. Designing smart contracts requires careful consideration of edge cases, clear failure modes, and well-defined access controls. The practical skill is to decide which operations require on-chain enforcement and to design contracts with events and interfaces that make off-chain integration straightforward. To deepen your understanding, inspect a simple contract: observe how functions change state and emit events that a frontend or indexer can consume. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Decentralized storage solutions like IPFS and Arweave let DApps keep large files and media off-chain while preserving decentralization and censorship resistance. Blockchains are poor places for bulky data because of cost and replication constraints; instead, DApps store content in peer-to-peer storage and record a content hash or pointer on-chain. For example, an NFT contract can store token metadata or art on IPFS and include the content identifier in the token's metadata field. This approach keeps ownership and provenance verifiable on-chain while avoiding high storage costs. A common mistake is trusting a single gateway or node to host content; decentralized storage requires content to be pinned or otherwise made widely available to ensure long-term persistence. Another practical point: content addressing via hashes provides integrity — if the content changes, the hash changes, so the on-chain pointer remains valid only for the original file. When designing storage for a DApp, decide which assets must be persistent and who or what will guarantee availability, such as pinning services or distributed incentives.
